title: Traffic & Road Safety
strapline: Red means stop, green means go — crossings, lollipop signs and learning to travel safely.
intent: Playing at traffic and crossings gives children safe, repeated practice of a genuinely important life skill — how to travel and cross roads safely.
Being the crossing patrol, driver or pedestrian, and obeying the lights, builds self-regulation, turn-taking and following rules that matter.
Traffic lights, signs and zebra crossings put print and symbol to work as real instructions children read and obey.
Reading signals, stopping and going on cue, and looking before crossing weave attention, listening and cause-and-effect into active play.
Talking about staying safe near roads, seatbelts and holding hands connects the play directly to children's real journeys.
Steering, pedalling and stopping ride-ons in a shared space builds physical control and awareness of others.
implementation: Mark out roads, a zebra crossing and junctions outdoors, and add ride-ons, a traffic light and a crossing patrol sign.
Play the game together — 'red, everybody stop!... green, off you go!' — and let children take turns controlling the lights.
Make and read the signs together — stop, go, crossing — as real instructions the drivers and walkers must follow.
Talk about crossing safely: 'stop, look, listen' — and practise it as a shared, repeatable routine.
Give roles — driver, pedestrian, lollipop person — and let children negotiate the busy junction cooperatively.
Connect it to real journeys and family rules about holding hands, seatbelts and looking both ways.
key_questions: Red, everybody stop! Green, off you go!
What does this sign tell the drivers to do?
How do we cross safely — stop, look and what next?
Whose turn is it to control the lights?
Why do we hold hands and look both ways on a real road?

impact.text: Children get safe, repeated practice of a genuinely important life skill — travelling and crossing safely.
Children obey the lights and take turns, building self-regulation and following rules that matter.
Children read traffic lights, signs and crossings as real instructions to follow.
Children steer, pedal and stop in a shared space, building physical control and awareness of others.
Children connect the play to real journeys and family rules about holding hands and seatbelts.

enhancements: Marked-out roads, a zebra crossing and junctions outdoors with ride-ons.
A traffic light children take turns to control.
Signs made and read together — stop, go, crossing.
Roles — driver, pedestrian, lollipop person — negotiated at a busy junction.
The 'stop, look, listen' routine practised as a shared habit.

playing_exploring: Children drive, walk and cross in a busy pretend world, testing the rules and the signals.
Ride-ons, lights and crossings pull children straight into an active, purposeful game.
active_learning: Stopping on red and holding still until green takes real self-control, and children rise to it because the game depends on it.
creating_thinking: Children read the signals and signs and work out what to do — when to stop, when it's safe to cross, how to keep the junction moving.
